The whitefin weakfish, Cynoscion albus, is a large sciaenid inhabiting the eastern Pacific from southern Baja California to Peru, and recent field surveys along the coast of Costa Rica have provided new data on its life history. Fertilized ova collected from plankton tows were measured, revealing a mean egg diameter of 0.72 mm, which corresponds to an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.0002 grams [Wwb = 0.0002 grams] for the yolk-sac larva immediately following eclosion. This minute starting mass reflects the small, pelagic egg typical of many tropical sciaenids and contrasts sharply with the species’ substantial asymptotic size. Indeed, adult females sampled from commercial catches attained an ultimate wet weight of 23,900 grams [Wwi = 23,900 grams], a value based on the empirical length–weight relationship derived for this stock. The ultimate total length of these individuals reached 130 centimeters [Li = 130 centimeters] from the tip of the snout to the caudal fin, placing Cynoscion albus among the larger members of the genus. These size metrics indicate a considerable scope for somatic growth over the lifespan.

The onset of sexual maturation in female Cynoscion albus is marked by a distinct size threshold, with puberty being attained at a total length of 72 centimeters [Lp = 72 centimeters] measured from the snout to the caudal fin. Correspondingly, the wet weight at puberty for females at this length is approximately 3,900 grams [Wwp = approximately 3,900 grams], a body mass that signifies the completion of a substantial juvenile growth phase. Histological examination of gonad tissue from individuals collected during the reproductive season confirmed that ovarian development and vitellogenesis onset occur once this size is reached, suggesting that length is a more reliable predictor of maturity than age in this population. The transition from the immature, post-metamorphic juvenile stage to the reproductively capable adult is thus tied to a critical body size, a pattern observed in other large, iteroparous sciaenids. Females below this threshold possess only undeveloped oogonia and remain incapable of spawning.

Reproductive output in whitefin weakfish is substantial, reflecting their large body size and position as a high-fecundity batch spawner. Based on comparisons with the congeneric spotted weakfish, Cynoscion nebulosus, females at a water temperature of 24.3 °C [T = 24.3 °C] exhibit a high daily reproductive rate of approximately 30,137 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 30,137 eggs per day] achieved through a combination of large clutch sizes and frequent spawning events. Specifically, a single mature female can produce approximately 30,137 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 30,137 eggs per clutch] with a spawning frequency of about one spawning event per day [F_R_i = about one spawning event per day] during the peak of the reproductive season. This daily spawning strategy is energetically demanding and is sustained only under favorable thermal conditions. The protracted spawning season, which spans several months in warm coastal waters, allows females to release multiple clutches sequentially, thereby maximizing annual fecundity.

Longevity data for Cynoscion albus, derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith annuli analysis, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 6,570 days [am = approximately 6,570 days] under natural conditions maintained at 24.3 °C [T = 24.3 °C]. This lifespan of about 18 years [am = about 18 years] is consistent with the pattern of slow growth and late maturity typical of large predators within the Scia at a temperature of 24.3 °C [T = 24.3 °C]enidae. The species exhibits an extended period of reproductive activity, beginning at the onset of puberty and continuing throughout most of adulthood, with no evidence of reproductive senescence in older individuals. The trade-off between rapid somatic growth in the early years and the subsequent allocation of resources toward reproduction is a defining feature of its life history strategy. Field records indicate that the oldest individuals, exceeding 20 years in age, have been caught in regions with cooler, upwelled water, suggesting that temperature plays a moderating role in the rate of physiological aging.

The ecological role of Cynoscion albus as a top predator is supported by its large adult dimensions; an asymptotic length of 130 centimeters [Li = 130 centimeters] and an adult body mass of 23,900 grams [Wwi = 23,900 grams] allow it to exploit a wide range of prey resources along the continental shelf. The minute larval mass at hatching, only 0.0002 grams [Wwb = 0.0002 grams], reflects the high vulnerability of early life stages to starvation and predation, factors that likely regulate recruitment in this species.
